# RustyNES v2.8.3 — "Rivet"

The fourth release of the v2.8.x line that [ADR 0041](https://github.com/doublegate/RustyNES/blob/main/docs/adr/0041-hardware-release-is-v3.0.0.md) put before the SuperStation One core (**v3.0.0**). v2.8.2 corrected what the MiSTer core computes; v2.8.3 makes it more robust in the ways a correctness gate cannot see: when its resets release, how much logic its CPU takes, and whether its comments tell the truth. Every row of the [RTL audit](https://github.com/doublegate/RustyNES/blob/main/docs/audits/rtl-audit-report.md) targeted here has a verdict and evidence in [its ledger](https://github.com/doublegate/RustyNES/blob/main/docs/audits/rtl-disposition.md).

**For emulator users:** nothing changes. **Everything here is the MiSTer core**, whose bitstream is attached below. **No hardware has run any bitstream**; that is v2.9.2's subject.

## Every reset released on its own clock

Every register in the core clears asynchronously, and the core's resets came straight from sources unrelated to the clocks that use them: the console's from an OR of the framework's reset, the menu, the button, the ROM download and the PLL's lock, and the SDRAM path's from the PLL's lock directly. Asserting a reset that way is harmless. Releasing it is not: across thousands of registers, a release near a clock edge can let part of the design start a cycle before the rest, which for this core would be a CPU/PPU phase error. The timing analysis could not see it either, and for the SDRAM clock it had no check at all.

A small synchroniser now releases each reset on a clock edge, one per clock and per source. The timing report now checks every release, and all of them pass:

| Clock | v2.8.2 | v2.8.3 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| SDRAM (`clk_sdram`) recovery / removal | not analysed | +5.201 ns / +1.415 ns |
| console (`clk_sys`) recovery / removal | +36.358 ns / +0.490 ns | +37.213 ns / +0.390 ns |

A new gate checks the release in simulation and runs the same test on the old wiring, which it shows releasing between clock edges in 4 of 4 placements. A simulation cannot show the routing delays that make the old wiring risky; the timing report is the evidence for that. A lint check reads the core's top level and fails if any reset input is driven by anything but a synchroniser, so a module added later cannot slip back onto a raw source unseen.

## A smaller CPU, measured one change at a time

The audit said two constructs in the core's 6502 were wasting logic, and put the cost at about 500 logic elements. The line plan's rule was to change them only if the fitter showed a real saving, so each was compiled on its own and read from the fit report, against a noise floor measured the same way (the unchanged CPU came out at 1,029.4 and 1,031.4 ALMs in two compiles).

| Change | CPU size | Why it is exact |
| --- | --- | --- |
| before | 1,031.4 ALMs | |
| the fetch path asks its three questions of a 3-bit table, not the whole decode | 999.6 | built by the same decode function |
| the read-modify-write address reuses an existing carry instead of a second 16-bit add | 987.3 | identical for all 2^24 inputs |

About 4%, an order of magnitude less than the audit's estimate. It is area only: the core's clock has about 13.9 ns of spare time.

## Comments that were wrong

Four comments in the core said something false and are corrected. The power-on CPU/PPU lead said "measured as 2" beside the correct value, 1. PAL was called "a parameter change" when the PPU hard-codes the NTSC frame. A pipeline depth of zero was described as working when it cannot be built. A superseded plan was cited as current. A block indented as if it ran once per dot, which it does not, is re-indented. Not one line of logic changed in that commit.

## The test harness

- **Run from a fresh checkout, the ladder silently skipped 19 gates**: two third-party batteries looked for their ROMs in the repository's own golden directory instead of the one the run was given, and the mapper ROMs were never built before the gates that need them. Both are fixed, so the ladder runs anywhere the goldens are, apart from one gate whose hand-built ROM no generator produces (documented, and passing where that ROM exists).
- A gate that checks each golden's ROM failed on a fresh checkout, because mapper ROMs are built after it runs; older mapper goldens only passed on this machine because they record absolute paths. It now builds the mapper ROMs itself and matches them by content.
- The ladder printed two gates as passing with an empty summary, the shape of a gate that checked nothing. Both now say what they compared, and no gate prints an empty summary.

## Verification

| Check | Result |
| --- | --- |
| Co-simulation ladder (`tb/regress.sh`), from a fresh checkout | 164 passed, 0 failed, 1 expected failure (`chrram-fetch`, unchanged); one documented skip, `ckpt:ppuspr0`, whose hand-built ROM no generator produces, and which passes where the ROM exists: 165 in all |
| `reset-sync-gate` | releases on edge 2 in 4 of 4 placements; the old wiring released between edges 4 of 4 times; both mutants caught |
| Quartus 17.0.2, fitter seed 4 | 0 errors, 0 warnings; worst setup +0.443 ns, worst hold +0.046 ns; 22,193 ALMs (CPU 977.5), 468 RAM blocks, 33 DSP |
| emulator | unchanged; its gates run in CI |

**Next: v2.8.4**, the off-die SDRAM build that v3.0.0 ships as its secondary bitstream.

## Install

- Download the pre-built binaries for Linux, macOS, and Windows below.
- The MiSTer core bitstream, `RustyNES_MiSTer-v2.8.3.rbf`, is attached below. It has not run on hardware.
- The WebAssembly build is live at [doublegate.github.io/RustyNES](https://doublegate.github.io/RustyNES/).
- The RetroArch core is in RetroArch's Online Updater on the platforms the libretro buildbot publishes to.
- The audit ledger is [`docs/audits/rtl-disposition.md`](https://github.com/doublegate/RustyNES/blob/main/docs/audits/rtl-disposition.md), and the plan [`to-dos/plans/v2.8.3-rivet-plan.md`](https://github.com/doublegate/RustyNES/blob/main/to-dos/plans/v2.8.3-rivet-plan.md).
